question: Does switch direction track NMD (PTC) status?
answer: Suggestive, NOT established -- direction consistent 4/4, significant 1/4
note: Within a gene the isoform gaining usage is more often an NMD target in all four datasets, but only T_UT reaches p<0.05 (21 vs 6). Sign test across the four is p=0.125. Pooling the three biological units gives 1.78x, p=0.020 -- but dropping T_UT alone collapses it to 1.29x, p=0.47, so the pool is largely that one dataset. T_HT, the same libraries re-annotated, leans the same way and does NOT reach significance, so the result is not even annotation-robust. Do not report as a finding without an independent dataset.

question: Does switch direction track intron retention?
answer: No -- null in every dataset, paired and unpaired
note: Paired riser-vs-faller is almost exactly balanced in all four datasets.

question: Are cryptic switchers functionally distinct (PTC/IR)?
note: Both markers, all four datasets, no difference beyond noise.

question: Is Class B enriched for NMD-target minor isoforms?
answer: No -- not enrichment, and not the transcripts being shed (answered 2026-08-27)
note: Testable since the context layer gained PTC (86-93% coverage vs 5-21%). Three readings, none supporting purification. (a) Minor isoforms ARE more often PTC+ than the dominant one -- but so are they in background genes (OR 75-319), so it is a property of being minor, not of Class B. (b) Minor-isoform PTC RATE in Class B vs background: 14.4/14.9% vs ~20% in T_HT/T_UT (depleted, p=0.012/0.042) and null in H_HT/U_UT -- and T_HT/T_UT are the SAME six libraries re-annotated, so that is one observation, not two. No enrichment anywhere. (c) Whether PTC predicts WHICH minors are shed: null in all four (p=0.27-0.98) once measured on dIF/IF1 and adjusted for baseline abundance. An earlier version of (c) used iso_lfc and reported a consistent four-of-four effect in the OPPOSITE direction; that was the +1 pseudocount acting on a class that is 1.5-4.1x less abundant (consequence_class_b_abundance_confound.csv), not biology.
